meta.subtitle: Solid-oxide fuel-cell power platform scaling on AI data-center demand; strong Q2'26, but the valuation has run ahead of the growth

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Bloom Energy a HOLD with a 12-month target range of $245 to $335. The company has reached an operating inflection: second-quarter 2026 revenue of $1,065.4 million rose {+ 165.5% +} year over year, and GAAP operating income of $182.2 million reversed a year-earlier operating loss. The business is now GAAP-operating-profitable and generating operating cash, funded by a large cash balance, and management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance. The problem is price, not performance. At $276.53 the shares carry premium multiples on every basis, the consensus target implies almost no upside, and the market already discounts several years of the AI-data-center power demand that drives the story. We see a genuine bull case if hyperscaler adoption keeps compounding, but the reward-to-risk from today's level is balanced rather than favorable, and a July 2026 short-seller report on the supply chain is a reminder that sentiment can turn quickly. We would wait for a better entry.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Bloom Energy Corporation designs, manufactures, sells, and installs solid-oxide fuel-cell systems for on-site power generation in the United States and internationally. Its primary product, the Bloom Energy Server, converts natural gas, biogas, hydrogen, or a blend of those fuels into electricity through a non-combustion electrochemical process; the company also offers the Bloom Electrolyzer for producing hydrogen. It sells through direct and indirect channels to utilities, data centers, retail, healthcare, education, telecom, and manufacturing customers. The company was incorporated in 2001, is headquartered in San Jose, California, and employs more than 2,000 people, manufacturing its systems in the United States.

Demand from AI data centers has become the central growth driver. Management states that all the major US hyperscalers and over a dozen US neoclouds, AI labs, and colocation data-center operators have validated and approved its power solutions. Revenue grew from $0.9 billion in FY21 to $2.0 billion in FY25 ({+ +38.9% +}), and the most recent quarter, Q2'26, delivered $1.1 billion of revenue, a quarterly level it had not reached before, per the company's press release. Bloom reports as a single reportable segment, so no product or geographic revenue split is disclosed here.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: The operating story has turned. Bloom moved from years of losses to GAAP operating income of $72.8 million in FY25, up from $22.9 million in FY24, and operating margin reached 17% in the most recent quarter as revenue scaled. AI data-center power demand is real, and management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance. But the valuation already reflects much of this. At $276.53 the stock trades at a triple-digit multiple on forward earnings, and the Street's consensus target implies almost no upside. For the shares to work from here, Bloom must keep compounding toward a steep FY27E consensus while defending margins, and the premium multiple must hold. We see balanced risk-reward: the bull case needs sustained hyperscaler adoption, while the bear case needs only a growth or sentiment wobble to compress a very high multiple. That balance supports a HOLD.

catalysts: Further raises to full-year 2026 guidance, or early FY27 commentary, if AI-data-center orders keep converting to revenue.
New hyperscaler, neocloud, or colocation wins that broaden the validated customer base beyond those already disclosed.
Evidence the Fremont capacity expansion is on schedule, supporting the volume and cost-reduction story.
Resolution of the July 2026 short-seller supply-chain allegations without financial impact, removing an overhang on sentiment.
Continued margin expansion and positive operating cash flow that carry the company toward GAAP net profitability.
risks: Extreme valuation: the shares carry premium, triple-digit forward multiples, so small disappointments can trigger large multiple compression.
AI-data-center demand could decelerate, and the customer base is concentrated among hyperscalers.
Supply-chain and raw-material questions, spotlighted by the July 2026 short-seller report, could resurface.
Policy risk: changes to tax credits, tax-equity financing, or tariffs could raise costs or cut demand.
The company remained net-loss-making in FY25 despite positive operating income, so profitability is not yet proven at the bottom line.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Bloom's income statement shows a multi-year margin inflection. Revenue rose from $0.9 billion in FY21 to $2.0 billion in FY25, with year-over-year growth accelerating from +13.6% in FY24 to {+ +38.9% +} in FY25. Gross margin widened from 15.6% in FY23 to 28.1% in FY24 and 29.3% in FY25 as volumes scaled. (The proxy's own 2025 summary reports FY25 revenue up 37.3% and gross margin of 29.0%, modestly below the vendor tearsheet series used here for consistency with the five-year table.) Operating income turned positive in FY24 and reached $72.8 million in FY25, {+ up $49.9 million +} from $22.9 million in FY24, lifting operating margin to 3.6% from 1.6%. The company was still net-loss-making in FY25 at {- -$88.4 million -} (diluted EPS -$0.37), because non-operating items sat between operating income and the bottom line.

The second quarter of 2026 extended the trend sharply. GAAP revenue was $1,065.4 million, up {+ 165.5% +} year over year, with product revenue of $935.4 million up {+ 215.4% +} (the snapshot header shows the rounded +168% from a different data feed; we use the press release's 165.5%). Gross margin reached 33.4%, up 668 basis points, and GAAP operating income was $182.2 million against a {- $3.5 million operating loss -} a year earlier. GAAP diluted EPS was $0.62 versus a loss of $(0.18). Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion, roughly 100% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
The balance sheet carries substantial cash and substantial debt. At FY25, cash and short-term investments were $2.5 billion against total debt of $2.6 billion, leaving net debt of just $0.2 billion; the current ratio was 5.98, up from 3.21 in FY24. The proxy explains the cash build: Bloom issued 0% notes at that scale in November 2025 and entered a $600 million revolving credit facility in December 2025, ending FY25 with the year-end cash balance above.

The most recent quarter shows the position holding. As of June 30, 2026, cash and cash equivalents were $2,666,859 thousand, up from $2,454,108 thousand at December 31, 2025; total current assets were $4,590,062 thousand against total current liabilities of $1,123,187 thousand, and long-term recourse debt was $2,470,704 thousand. Total stockholders' equity attributable to common stockholders more than doubled to $1,611,998 thousand from $768,641 thousand, as the accumulated deficit narrowed to $(3,720,965) thousand and additional paid-in capital rose to $5,332,587 thousand. Trailing interest coverage was 8.2x. The zero-coupon note structure keeps cash interest low, but the gross debt load and the accumulated deficit are reminders that this is still a capital-intensive business scaling into demand.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation has only recently turned positive. Operating cash flow was negative every year from FY21 through FY23, reaching -$0.4 billion in FY23, before turning to +$0.1 billion in both FY24 and FY25. Free cash flow followed the same path, from -$0.5 billion in FY23 to positive $0.1 billion in FY25 (an FCF margin of 2.9%), with capital expenditure held near $0.1 billion a year. The proxy notes FY25 marked the second consecutive year of positive free cash flow, with $113.9 million of cash flow from operations, up 23% over FY24.

The second quarter of 2026 brought a sharp cash improvement: cash flow from operating activities was $226.4 million, {+ a $439.5 million improvement +} from $213.1 million of net cash used a year earlier. Trailing free-cash-flow yield remains thin at 0.8%, consistent with a business still investing to scale and valued richly. The dividend yield is 0.00%; the company pays no dividend and reports no share repurchases.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The valuation is the crux of the call. At $276.53 the shares trade at 363.9x trailing earnings, 26.3x sales, and 102.2x next-twelve-month earnings; on FY27E EPS of $4.93 the forward multiple is about 56.1x. EV/EBITDA is not shown because a trailing EBITDA figure is not available in the pack. These are premium multiples for any company, and they embed years of the growth that the AI-data-center thesis promises.

The Street is divided despite a Buy consensus. Of 29 analysts, 15 rate the stock Buy, 12 Hold, and 2 Sell. The consensus price target is $280.24 (+1.3% from the current price) and the median is $296.50, but the range runs from $97.00 to $390.00 — a spread that captures both a multiple that keeps expanding and one that compresses hard. With trailing net margin at 7.9% and TTM operating margin at 11.3%, the company must convert its raised guidance into sustained earnings to grow into these multiples rather than de-rate toward them.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: AI data-center power demand keeps compounding and Bloom hits the high end of its raised FY26 guidance (non-GAAP EPS of $2.85) on its way toward a steep FY27E consensus. Hyperscaler and neocloud adoption broadens, non-GAAP operating income reaches the guided range, and the market keeps paying a premium multiple for durable, scarce on-site power. The short-seller supply-chain claims fade without financial impact.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Bloom executes to the midpoint of its FY26 guidance and grows toward the FY27E consensus, but the multiple compresses as much of the growth is already priced. The stock tracks near the Street's consensus and median targets, advancing only modestly even as the business delivers.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: AI data-center capex slows or Bloom's growth decelerates, and the July 2026 short-seller report keeps sentiment fragile. A very high multiple compresses sharply on any disappointment, and the shares fall back toward the lower half of the 52-week range of $61.37 to $351.28. Tariffs and freight costs pressure margins.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Our probability-weighted fair value sits close to the current price, which is why we land on HOLD rather than a directional call. We weight the Base case at 45%: Bloom delivers on its raised guidance and grows toward the FY27E consensus, but a multiple this high leaves little room for the stock to advance even as the business does. We give the Bull case 30% because the AI-data-center demand signal is genuine and management says the major US hyperscalers have validated its solutions; if that adoption compounds, the premium can persist and the shares can approach the upper end of the Street's target range. We give the Bear case 25% and place its implied price well below the current level because a triple-digit forward multiple compresses violently on any growth or sentiment shock, and the July 2026 short-seller report shows how quickly confidence can wobble. The target range of $245 to $335 brackets the Base case and reflects the wide dispersion in the Street's own targets.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Bloom reports as a single reportable segment, so the pack shows only the consolidated total and no product or geographic split. The business rests on two product lines. The Bloom Energy Server, its primary product, is a proprietary high-temperature solid-oxide fuel-cell system that converts natural gas, biogas, or hydrogen into electricity without combustion or moving parts, at high density and with lower emissions than legacy systems; it serves on-site power for data centers, utilities, semiconductor manufacturing, hospitals, campuses, and retailers, and it is the engine of the recent revenue scaling. The Bloom Electrolyzer produces hydrogen, extending the platform into the energy transition, and is an earlier-stage line.

moatFactors.name: Proprietary solid-oxide technology
moatFactors.body: Bloom's high-temperature solid-oxide fuel-cell technology converts multiple fuels to electricity without combustion, and management describes it as proprietary. The technology and the manufacturing know-how create a real barrier, though distributed generation and hydrogen production are described in the 10-K as emerging markets that may not receive widespread acceptance.

moatFactors.name: Hyperscaler validation and switching costs
moatFactors.body: The hyperscaler validation noted earlier matters here: once a data-center operator designs Bloom systems into a site, the lengthy sales, interconnection, and installation cycle raises switching costs and locks in multi-year deployment. Backlog rose 2.5x year over year in FY25 per the proxy, evidence of committed demand that competitors would have to displace.

moatFactors.name: US manufacturing scale
moatFactors.body: Bloom manufactures its systems in the United States and plans to double its Fremont annual production run rate from 1GW to 2GW by the end of 2026, with room to scale to 5GW. Scale supports the cost reductions needed to defend margins, but the 10-K flags that increasing production capacity is itself a risk.

moatFactors.name: Competition and input dependence
moatFactors.body: The 10-K states Bloom faces significant competition and relies on some sole-source suppliers and on scarce raw materials; a July 2026 short-seller report questioned the sufficiency of certain raw materials, which the company rejected. Tariffs and freight volatility add cost pressure. These factors cap the moat at narrow.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow rather than wide. The technology is proprietary and hyperscaler validation is a strong endorsement, but the end markets are still emerging, competition is significant, and the business depends on suppliers, incentives, and financing to deploy high-upfront-cost systems. Government incentives matter: the 10-K flags reliance on rebates, tax credits, tax-equity financing, and programs such as the IRA and the OBBBA, any change to which could reduce demand. Durability therefore rests on Bloom continuing to cut costs, expand capacity on plan, and convert AI-data-center interest into installed base faster than competitors, while keeping its supply chain and incentives intact. The recent margin inflection and backlog growth support the case; the emerging-market and policy dependence are what keep it from being wide.

points: AI data-center power demand is the primary driver. The 10-K names a rising AI customer mix as a growth factor, and management reports broad hyperscaler and neocloud validation of Bloom's solutions, detailed in the overview.
Management lifted its full-year 2026 outlook; non-GAAP operating income is now guided to $800 million to $900 million, on the raised revenue range.
The consensus growth path is steep: FY26E revenue of $4.1 billion rising to FY27E revenue of $6.8 billion. Meeting it is what the current premium multiple already assumes.

Bloom is shifting to a consult-only installation model for large-load sites, using certified third-party installers while it acts as consultant; this can help it scale deployments without expanding its own installation labor in step.

The product platform can broaden. Beyond the Energy Server, the Bloom Electrolyzer targets hydrogen production, extending the addressable market into the energy transition, though it is earlier-stage.

management.leadership: KR Sridhar is Founder, Chairman, and Chief Executive Officer and set the strategy of making Bloom the standard for on-site power. Simon Edwards is Chief Financial Officer and, in the Q2'26 release, framed the quarter as the strongest in the company's history with profitable growth and positive operating cash flow. The proxy shows recent turnover in the finance function: Daniel Berenbaum departed as CFO effective May 1, 2025, and Maciej Kurzymski, Chief Accounting Officer, served as Acting Principal Financial Officer from May 2, 2025; the July 2026 release identifies Simon Edwards as CFO, indicating the role has since been filled. Other named executives include Satish Chitoori (Chief Operations Officer), Aman Joshi (Chief Commercial Officer), and Shawn M. Soderberg (Chief Legal Officer and Corporate Secretary). The team has delivered the operating inflection, and the recent CFO transition is the main continuity question to watch.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is oriented to growth and balance-sheet strength, not shareholder returns. Bloom pays no dividend (yield 0.00%) and reports no share repurchases. In late 2025 it raised $2.5 billion through 0% notes and added a $600 million revolving credit facility, ending FY25 with a cash balance of similar size against $2.6 billion of total debt, so net debt was only $0.2 billion. That cash funds the capacity expansion described under the moat section. Capital expenditure has stayed near $0.1 billion a year even as revenue scaled, and free cash flow turned positive in FY24 and FY25. The zero-coupon structure limits cash interest while the company invests, but it does add gross leverage that must be serviced or refinanced as the business matures. We view the priorities as appropriate for a company scaling into demand, provided execution holds.
management.governance: Governance rests on the proxy statement in the pack. The Board has determined that all continuing directors and nominees are independent under NYSE listing standards other than the CEO, who is not independent as an employee, and that all members of the Audit and Compensation Committees meet the additional independence requirements. Bloom maintains a written Related Party Transaction Policy under which transactions above $120,000 involving a related party require Audit Committee review and approval. Related-party relationships disclosed include a variable interest entity tied to a joint venture in the Republic of Korea and investments in joint ventures with Brookfield Asset Management. One governance consideration is the combined Chairman and CEO role held by KR Sridhar. On executive pay, the Compensation Committee in 2025 replaced the non-GAAP operating gross margin metric with total revenue, retained non-GAAP operating income, raised the maximum annual cash incentive earn-out from 1.5x to 2x target, and adopted an updated peer group reflecting the AI-infrastructure talent market.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is modest but real. As of February 27, 2026, CEO KR Sridhar beneficially owned 5,662,140 shares (2.0%), and all directors and executive officers as a group (14 persons) owned 8,339,993 shares (3.0%) of Class A common stock. Institutional ownership is concentrated among large managers: Ameriprise Financial held 30,147,240 shares (10.7%) and BlackRock 22,345,779 shares (7.9%), each per recent Schedule 13G/A filings. The proxy also lists The Vanguard Group, but that figure derives from a filing dated December 2023 and Vanguard has since disclaimed beneficial ownership, so it is not treated here as a current holding. The proxy notes that, following the 2025 Equity Package and Replacement Grant made in December 2024, Dr. Sridhar received no additional equity in 2025. A single share class simplifies the structure after the May 27, 2026 amendment that renamed Class A common stock as common stock and eliminated references to Class B stock.

idiosyncratic: Valuation. At a triple-digit forward multiple, the stock prices in years of growth; any disappointment against the raised FY26 guidance or a steep FY27E consensus could compress the multiple sharply, and the Street's consensus target already sits barely above the current price.

Short-seller report and supply chain. On July 8, 2026 a short seller published allegations about Bloom's supply chain and the sourcing and sufficiency of certain raw materials; the company rejected the conclusions in a July 9, 2026 8-K but noted the report caused significant stock-price volatility and ongoing response costs. The 10-K separately flags reliance on sole-source suppliers.

AI-demand concentration. Growth is increasingly tied to AI data centers; the 10-K warns that a slower expansion of AI data centers, from actual or perceived deceleration in AI adoption, could adversely affect results. A customer base skewed to hyperscalers concentrates demand.

Incentives and policy. Bloom relies on rebates, tax credits, and tax-equity financing, and on programs such as the IRA and the OBBBA; the 10-K flags that changes to these benefits could cut revenue. Import tariffs announced in late July 2026 and freight volatility add cost pressure.

Profitability quality. The company was still net-loss-making in FY25 (-$88.4 million) despite positive operating income, and free-cash-flow yield is thin at 0.8%; margins depend on continued cost reduction against commodity, tariff, and wage inflation.
risks.systemic: Systemic risks are macro and policy-driven. Bloom's demand depends on the price and availability of natural gas and electricity, on the pace of AI-data-center buildout, and on government energy incentives that can change with administrations. The MD&A flags freight and logistics volatility, commodity-price swings in steel, aluminum, copper, and rare-earth-dependent materials, and persistent inflation in parts and skilled labor, all of which can pressure margins. Trade policy is a live factor: after a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling against certain IEEPA tariffs, the administration imposed new tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on imports from approximately 60 economies in late July 2026, covering almost all US imports and Bloom's imported inputs. Broad equity-market multiple compression would hit a stock trading at a triple-digit forward multiple harder than the average name. These are largely outside management's control.

body: We come out at HOLD on Bloom Energy, framing a 12-month target range of $245 to $335. The operating turn is real: Q2'26 revenue topped $1 billion, GAAP operating income swung firmly positive, and management raised its full-year 2026 guidance. But at $276.53 the shares already trade at a triple-digit forward multiple, the Street's consensus target sits essentially flat to the price, and our probability-weighted fair value sits close to today's price.

The path to owning it is a better price or clearer evidence that the steep FY27E consensus is conservative. The bull case — sustained AI-data-center adoption at a premium multiple — is genuine, but the bear case needs only a growth or sentiment shock, of the kind the July 2026 short-seller report produced, to compress a very high multiple. Balanced reward-to-risk from this level supports waiting rather than buying, and holding rather than selling a business executing this well.
